comparisons.interpretation: Sanders proposes a national single-payer program free at point of service. Yang's current policy discussion supports Medicare for All's spirit while rejecting rapid elimination of private coverage and prioritizing cost and delivery reform. A shared page title or older embedded quote is not an identical insurance design.

Sanders specifies a stable living-wage employment guarantee; Yang specifies a monthly cash income independent of work. These are distinct income-security mechanisms, but these excerpts do not prove either rejects all versions of the other's tool.

Sanders foregrounds building a justice-oriented movement; Yang frames an economic-system upgrade around human wellbeing and markets serving common values. Endorsement is not used to impute an unquoted theory of ownership.

Sanders specifies universal national single-payer insurance. Gleib combines Medicare expansion for uninsured people, ACA repair, private choice and ending job-tied coverage. Both state access goals, with different institutional routes.

Sanders guarantees tuition/debt-free public institutions and additional cost support. Gleib proposes a free accredited online university with optional in-person activities rather than funding all conventional attendance costs.
Sanders proposes canceling all existing student debt; Gleib proposes forgiving half and easing repayment of the remainder. The scope difference is explicit.

Sanders' selected section gives a renewable-energy endpoint and investment program; Gleib foregrounds Paris reentry, a stronger agreement and Green New Deal principles. The tools and goal are not inherently incompatible.
Both explicitly propose ending private or for-profit prisons. Their other criminal-justice proposals are not assumed identical.
Both affirm fully/properly funding the VA. Sanders additionally specifies staffing and anti-privatization measures; Gleib gives a first-year funding pledge.

Sanders describes a movement for interlocking justice goals; Gleib explicitly describes compassionate capitalism and a safety net. Gleib's own ideological label is preserved without assigning Sanders an unquoted label from DSA membership alone.

Sanders specifies a single-payer mechanism; Patrick's vision page affirms universal quality and low-cost access without defining insurance financing. Missing detail is not a rejection of single payer.

Sanders specifies a tuition/debt-free guarantee; Patrick foregrounds investment from pre-K through community college and workforce training. The broader investment language does not establish opposition to tuition-free college.

Sanders foregrounds movement-building for justice; Patrick foregrounds long-term opportunity, reform and democracy rather than news-cycle politics. These are stated frames, not measured campaign spending or effectiveness.

The selected Sanders passage specifies tenant regulation; Bullock specifies shared equity, land trusts and minority homeownership. Sanders' full source also proposes major construction and public investment, so this is not a regulation-versus-supply binary.

Sanders specifies teacher pay, bargaining and classroom support; Bullock states an aggregate K-12 funding expansion. These are different stated investment tools, not directly comparable budget multipliers or opposing commitments.

Sanders proposes national single-payer insurance. Williamson's dedicated healthcare page explicitly offers Medicare on ACA exchanges with private choice and anticipated migration toward Medicare. General Medicare-for-all wording elsewhere does not erase that specific route.
Both explicitly support canceling all existing college/student-loan debt. Their other education policies and financing details remain separate.

Both advocate tuition-free public higher education. Sanders explicitly adds a universal debt-free guarantee and non-tuition supports; Williamson's selected line specifies free public tuition while other text foregrounds those unable to afford it. The source does not settle every eligibility or living-cost detail.

Sanders specifies an employment guarantee; Williamson specifies a cash basic income in addition to service and education proposals. Her page's all-adults versus18-65 wording remains unresolved, and neither excerpt proves blanket opposition to the other's mechanism.

Both propose taxing high net worth, but Sanders' quoted threshold begins above$32million while Williamson's embedded response starts above$50million and specifies two rates. This comparison does not invent the rest of Sanders' rate schedule or claim a measured revenue effect.

Both mobilize citizens around change. Sanders foregrounds a movement for economic, racial, social and environmental justice; Williamson foregrounds moral and civic renewal and a contrast between love and fear.
